overview: This four-page “List of Papers” is an internal register for State Department file 894C.77, “Railways—Kwantung,” indexing items 2–35 and several related outgoing instructions from the 1930s. It documents American diplomatic reporting on the South Manchuria Railway Company’s purchasing, contractors, accounts, budgets, employment, construction projects, subsidiaries, management changes, and repeated reorganizations, particularly its transfer of functions to Changchun and its relationship with the Kwantung Army. Other subjects include Chinese railway and harbor competition, Japanese claims before the League of Nations, railway agreements within Manchuria, and a 1939 diplomatic dispute over undelivered locomotive parts consigned to the Peiping–Suiyuan Railway. The underlying telegrams, despatches, clippings, translations, and enclosures are not present in this OCR, but the register identifies and summarizes them and records several cross-references to other decimal files.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Railways—Kwantung, items 2–35
subfiles.about: Four-page register indexing diplomatic papers concerning the South Manchuria Railway Company, railway affairs in the Kwantung Leased Territory, and related Sino-Japanese transportation questions during the 1930s.
subfiles.summary: The register indexes telegrams, despatches, notes, clippings, translations, and cross-references concerning the South Manchuria Railway Company’s purchases, contractors, finances, construction plans, employment, subsidiaries, management, and reorganization. It records reporting on the proposed Dairen station, Yōsuke Matsuoka’s appointment, the transfer of the company’s head office to Changchun, unification of Manchurian railway control, and the company’s relationship with the Kwantung Army. Additional entries concern Chinese railway and harbor competition, the Chinchow–Pitsuwo and Peiping–Mukden railways, and Japanese representations to the League of Nations. The final sequence traces October 1939 communications about undelivered locomotive parts for the Peiping–Suiyuan Railway and instructions to approach Chinese officials without disclosing earlier representations to Japanese authorities.

interest: The register is valuable as a roadmap to a larger and partly dispersed documentary record, since it identifies papers cross-filed under Manchurian political, military, and railway subjects and notes otherwise elusive enclosures such as newspaper clippings, corporate articles, and financial statements. It shows that American officials regarded the South Manchuria Railway as much more than a transportation company: it was simultaneously a commercial enterprise, an administrative structure, and a strategic instrument closely entangled with the Kwantung Army. The 1939 locomotive-parts entries are especially revealing about the delicacy of dealing simultaneously with Chinese and Japanese authorities and the Department’s effort to keep the two approaches compartmentalized.
